intro: Christians agree that Jesus will come again, raise the dead and gather his people (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). They disagree on three linked questions. First, when are believers 'caught up' to meet the Lord: before, in the middle of, late in, or at the end of a future time of trouble, or at one single return with no seven-year period at all? Second, what is the thousand-year reign of Revelation 20:1-6: the present age of Christ's rule from heaven (amillennial), a coming golden age of gospel success (postmillennial), or a future reign on earth after his return (historic and dispensational premillennial)? Third, what is the church's task toward God's kingdom: to wait for Christ to establish a literal kingdom at his coming, or to steward a kingdom he already established at his resurrection (Matthew 28:18-20)? Many positions sit between these two ends. This study sets out each view as its best defenders present it, with their key texts, their arguments, the strongest counters and their answers. It traces how each view arose in church history, and it closes with the common ground that all of them share.

tribViews.name: Pre-tribulation rapture
tribViews.summary: Christ comes for his church before the seven-year tribulation begins. Believers are caught up to heaven and later return with him at his visible coming to earth. The tribulation is Daniel's seventieth week, a time of God's wrath focused on Israel and the nations. The rapture can happen at any moment, with no prophesied sign before it.
tribViews.timing: The rapture opens the seven years (0). Pretribulationists hold that the whole seventieth week is the day of the Lord, so wrath begins with the first seal (Revelation 6:1). The church is absent from all of it and returns with Christ at year 7.
tribViews.origin: Taught systematically by John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren from the 1830s. Spread in America through prophecy conferences, the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and Dallas Theological Seminary. Proponents point to earlier hints, such as Pseudo-Ephraem and Morgan Edwards, but how much these teach the view is disputed.
tribViews.strengths: It explains the promise that believers are not appointed to wrath and the call to expect Christ at any moment. It keeps the distinction between Israel and the church that dispensationalists find in Daniel 9:24-27. It notes that the church is not named on earth in Revelation 4-18.
tribViews.weaknesses: Critics answer that no single text places the rapture before the tribulation. Jesus and Paul seem to describe one gathering after the tribulation (Matthew 24:29-31; 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3). Many see the view as a nineteenth-century development. Defenders reply that the doctrine is built from several texts together and that age does not decide truth.

tribViews.name: Mid-tribulation rapture
tribViews.summary: The church is caught up at the midpoint of the seven years, when the Antichrist breaks his covenant (Daniel 9:27). The first half holds human and satanic trouble that the church endures. The second half, the great tribulation, is God's wrath, from which the church is removed.
tribViews.timing: The rapture comes at 3.5 years. Many link Paul's 'last trump' (1 Corinthians 15:52) with the seventh trumpet (Revelation 11:15) and the rising of the two witnesses (Revelation 11:11-12). Divine wrath fills the second half, from 3.5 to 7.
tribViews.origin: Developed in the twentieth century among premillennialists who doubted both a pre- and a post-tribulation rapture. Norman B. Harrison (1941) and J. Oliver Buswell (1962) gave it its main form. Gleason Archer defended a related view in the 1984 Three Views book.
tribViews.strengths: It takes seriously the recurring half-week (time, times and half a time) in Daniel and Revelation. It accepts that the church suffers tribulation while still holding that it escapes wrath. It offers a link between the 'last trumpet' texts.
tribViews.weaknesses: Critics from both sides note that Revelation's seventh trumpet is part of a judgment series, not a gathering signal. They argue that wrath begins earlier (the sixth seal) or later (at the return). Few current scholars defend it. Supporters answer that the midpoint is the clearest structural break in the prophecy.

tribViews.name: Pre-wrath rapture
tribViews.summary: The church will face the Antichrist's persecution in the great tribulation. That persecution is cut short when Christ comes, after the sun, moon and stars are darkened, to gather his elect. The day of the Lord's wrath then begins and runs to the end of the seventieth week.
tribViews.timing: The rapture falls at an unknown point in the second half, shown here as about 5.25 years. It follows the cosmic signs of the sixth seal (Revelation 6:12-17; Matthew 24:29-31). God's wrath, the trumpets and bowls, begins at once after it with the seventh seal.
tribViews.origin: Formulated by Robert Van Kampen and popularised by Marvin Rosenthal, who left a pretribulational ministry and published The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church (1990). Van Kampen's The Sign (1992) gave the full system. Alan Kurschner and Alan Hultberg have given it academic defence.
tribViews.strengths: It separates human persecution from God's wrath, as many texts do. It follows the order of Jesus' Olivet sermon closely: tribulation, cosmic signs, then gathering. It explains the great multitude that comes 'out of the great tribulation' (Revelation 7:14).
tribViews.weaknesses: Pretribulationists argue that the seals are God's wrath from the start, since the Lamb opens them. Posttribulationists argue that Matthew 24:29-31 describes the final return, not a separate rapture. Defenders reply that the text first mentions wrath only at the sixth seal (Revelation 6:17).

tribViews.name: Post-tribulation rapture
tribViews.summary: The church goes through the tribulation and is gathered at the single, visible return of Christ at its end. Believers rise to meet the Lord in the air and escort him back to earth, as citizens went out to meet an arriving king. God protects his people through the trouble, as he protected Israel in Egypt.
tribViews.timing: The rapture comes at year 7, at the visible return. Posttribulationists hold that God's full wrath falls on the wicked at the return itself (2 Thessalonians 1:7-9). Judgments during the tribulation fall on unbelievers while believers are kept through them (John 17:15).
tribViews.origin: Most early Christian writers, such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus, expected the church to face the Antichrist before Christ returns. In modern times it was revived against Darby by B. W. Newton, then by Alexander Reese (1937), George Eldon Ladd (1956), Robert Gundry (1973) and Douglas Moo.
tribViews.strengths: It reads Jesus' and Paul's gathering texts in their most direct order. It has strong support in the early church. Its reading of the Greek word for 'meeting' (apantēsis) in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 fits the escort custom. It names one second coming, not two stages.
tribViews.weaknesses: Pretribulationists answer that it loses the any-moment hope and leaves no unglorified believers to enter and populate the millennium. They also ask why believers are lifted up only to return at once. Posttribulationists reply that the millennium's people come from survivors who turn to Christ, and the hope is Christ's appearing, not escape.

tribViews.name: Partial rapture
tribViews.summary: Only watchful, faithful believers are caught up before the tribulation. Other true believers, who are not ready, remain on earth to be purified and are taken later, during or at the end of it. The rapture is a reward for readiness, not a part of salvation itself.
tribViews.timing: Watchful believers are taken at the start (0), and wrath begins then. Other believers are gathered in later raptures during the seven years or at Christ's return at year 7. Proponents differ on how many stages there are.
tribViews.origin: Taught by Robert Govett in England from the 1850s, then by G. H. Pember, D. M. Panton and G. H. Lang. Watchman Nee spread the view in China. It has always been a minority view.
tribViews.strengths: It takes seriously the many warnings to watch and be ready, and texts that tie being 'counted worthy' to escape (Luke 21:36). It explains why the parables include unready servants and virgins.
tribViews.weaknesses: Critics say it divides the body of Christ, which Paul says is raised as one: 'the dead in Christ' and 'we who are alive' (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17; 1 Corinthians 15:51). They argue that it bases the rapture on works, not grace. Proponents reply that salvation is by grace, while reward and timing depend on faithfulness.

tribViews.name: One coming, no future seven years
tribViews.summary: There is one future return of Christ, visible and glorious. At it the dead are raised, the living are changed and caught up, and the final judgment follows. Daniel's seventieth week is fulfilled in Christ's first coming or the events around AD 70, so no future seven-year tribulation exists. The church suffers tribulation throughout this age.
tribViews.timing: No future seven-year period exists, so the view has no place on this scale. The 'catching up' happens at Christ's single return at the end of history (John 6:40). Tribulation marks the whole time between Christ's two comings. God's final wrath falls at the last day.
tribViews.origin: This was the dominant view of the church from Augustine through the Reformation. It remains standard in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed teaching. It is held by most amillennialists, postmillennialists and preterists.
tribViews.strengths: It reads the New Testament as teaching one return, one resurrection of all and one judgment (John 5:28-29). It has the deepest history in the creeds and the church. It does not depend on a gap between Daniel's sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks.
tribViews.weaknesses: Futurists argue that it does not explain Revelation's detailed sequence or the unique 'great tribulation' Jesus foretold (Matthew 24:21). Premillennialists argue that Revelation 20 places two resurrections a thousand years apart. Proponents reply that Revelation repeats its visions, so it does not set out a strict timeline.

texts.title: Caught up to meet the Lord in the air
texts.question: When believers rise to "meet" the Lord in the air, do they go with him to heaven, or do they turn and escort him back to earth?

readings.reading: This is the clearest rapture text. Paul gives no signs and no tribulation before it, and he offers it as comfort (verse 18). Pretribulationists hold that Christ takes the church to the Father's house (John 14:2-3) and returns with it seven years later. The word "meet" does not by itself say which way the party moves after the meeting.

Midtribulationists agree that this is a gathering to heaven, separate from the return to earth. They place it at the middle of the week, linked to the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52, which they connect with the seventh trumpet in Revelation 11.

Prewrath writers read this as the same event as the gathering of the elect in Matthew 24:31: the same descent, trumpet, clouds and angels. It happens after the Antichrist is revealed and the cosmic signs appear, but before God's wrath falls on the earth.

Posttribulationists stress the word apantesis. In Greek use it often described citizens going out to meet a visiting ruler and then escorting him back into the city (compare Acts 28:15). Believers rise to meet Christ and return with him at once to earth.

Partial-rapture writers agree that this is a rapture before the tribulation, but note that it is for "the dead in Christ" and those who are his. They read other texts (Luke 21:36, Hebrews 9:28) to mean that only watchful believers are taken at this stage.

Amillennial and postmillennial writers read the trumpet, the voice and the cloud as one public, visible event, the single return of Christ at the end of the age. The meeting in the air leads straight to the resurrection, the judgment and the new creation.

texts.title: Not appointed to wrath
texts.question: Does "God has not appointed us to wrath" mean believers are removed before the tribulation, or only that they escape God's final judgment?

readings.reading: Paul moves straight from the rapture (4:13-18) to "the day of the Lord" (5:1-3) and says believers are not destined for wrath. Pretribulationists hold that the whole seventieth week is the day of the Lord and is full of divine wrath (Revelation 6:16-17), so the church must be removed before it begins.

Midtribulationists say the wrath of God is poured out in the second half of the week, especially in the trumpets and bowls. The first half is the wrath of man and Satan. So the church is removed at the middle, before divine wrath begins.

Prewrath writers agree that believers are exempt from God's wrath, but separate it from the "great tribulation", which is the Antichrist's persecution. God's wrath starts only after the sixth seal (Revelation 6:17), so the church endures persecution and is rescued before the trumpets.

Posttribulationists read "wrath" as God's final judgment on the lost, contrasted with "salvation" in the same verse. God can protect his people in the midst of judgment, as he did Israel in Goshen (Exodus 8:22). The verse promises rescue from wrath, not removal from trouble.
Partial-rapture writers say the promise holds for those who are watchful and sober (5:6-8). Believers who are spiritually asleep may face part of the time of testing, though not eternal wrath.

On this view the wrath is the final judgment at Christ's one return. Paul's contrast is between eternal wrath and eternal salvation through Christ (compare 1 Thessalonians 1:10), not between two stages of future history.

texts.title: The last trumpet
texts.question: Is the "last trumpet" the last trumpet of all, the seventh trumpet of Revelation, or simply the signal that closes the church age?

readings.reading: Pretribulationists say "last" means the final trumpet for the church, a call to gather God's people, as in the Roman army or Israel's camp (Numbers 10:2-6). It need not be the last trumpet in all prophecy, and Paul wrote before Revelation's trumpets were known.

Midtribulationists identify Paul's last trumpet with the seventh trumpet (Revelation 11:15), which they place near the middle of the week. At that trumpet the kingdom is announced and the dead are judged and rewarded (Revelation 11:18).

Prewrath writers usually do not equate this trumpet with the seventh trumpet of Revelation. They link it to the trumpet that gathers the elect in Matthew 24:31, sounded after the cosmic signs and before the day of the Lord's wrath.

Posttribulationists take "last" at face value. If it is the last trumpet, it cannot sound seven years before other trumpets. They link it with the great trumpet of Matthew 24:31, which is clearly after the tribulation.
Partial-rapture writers accept a rapture at a trumpet but hold that later raptures of other believers can still occur during the tribulation. They give less weight to the word "last".

On this view the last trumpet ends history. It sounds once, at the single coming, when all the dead are raised and the living changed. Nothing in the passage suggests further trumpets or a later stage.

texts.title: I will come again and receive you
texts.question: Does Jesus promise to take his people to the Father's house in heaven, or to come and dwell with them?

readings.reading: Pretribulationists see a clear sequence: Jesus goes to prepare a place, comes back, and takes his disciples to where he is, the Father's house. This fits a coming for the church that takes it to heaven, not a coming to earth to set up the kingdom.
Midtribulationists share the pretribulational reading: the church is taken to heaven while judgment falls on the earth in the second half of the week.
Prewrath writers agree that Jesus takes his people to be with him. They note the text gives no timing, and they place the event after the sixth seal.

Posttribulationists reply that the text says nothing about a seven-year stay in heaven. "Where I am" can mean with Christ wherever he is. In John 14:23 the Father and Son come to make their home with believers, which points to God dwelling with his people, not a removal.

Many in this group read the "rooms" as a place with God secured by Christ's death and resurrection. Some see a present fulfilment in the Spirit's coming (John 14:18, 14:23); all see a final fulfilment at the one return, ending in the new creation where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:3).

texts.title: Kept from the hour of trial
texts.question: Does "keep you from (tereo ek) the hour of trial" mean removal before the hour, or protection through it?

readings.reading: The promise is to be kept from the hour itself, not just the trial. Pretribulationists argue that the only way to be kept from a period of time that comes on the whole world is to be removed from it. The hour is world-wide and aimed at "those who dwell on the earth".
Midtribulationists apply the promise to the hour of God's wrath in the second half of the week. The church is kept from that hour by a rapture at the middle.
Prewrath writers say the hour of trial is the day of the Lord's wrath, which begins after the sixth seal. The church is kept from that hour by being gathered just before it.

Gundry and others note that the same phrase "keep from" (tereo ek) is used in John 17:15, where Jesus asks the Father not to take his disciples out of the world but to keep them from the evil one. So it means protection while present, not removal.
Partial-rapture writers stress that the promise is a reward: "because you have kept my word". Only faithful, watchful believers are kept from the hour. This is a main text for their view.

On this view the promise was first to the church at Philadelphia, facing a real trial in its own day. It also teaches that God guards his people spiritually in every trial. It does not describe a future seven-year period.

texts.title: "Come up here" and the church in chapters 4-19
texts.question: Does John's call to "come up here" picture the rapture, and is the church truly absent from Revelation 4-19?

readings.reading: The word "church" appears nineteen times in chapters 1-3 and not again until 22:16. Pretribulationists read this as a sign that the church is in heaven during the judgments of chapters 6-19. Many see the twenty-four elders (4:4) as the raptured church, crowned and enthroned. Most do not claim that 4:1 itself is the rapture.
Midtribulationists agree the church is in heaven during the later judgments, but place its arrival at chapter 11 rather than chapter 4.
Prewrath writers say the church is on earth during the seals and is seen as the great multitude arriving in heaven in 7:9-14, "out of the great tribulation", just before the trumpets.

Posttribulationists reply that "come up here" is said to John alone, as a prophet. The word "church" is also missing from many New Testament books and from heaven in chapters 4-19. Saints, servants, and those who keep the commands of God and the testimony of Jesus (12:17) appear on earth throughout.

Amillennial writers see chapter 4 as a new vision of the throne room that frames the whole age. Revelation repeats the same period from different angles, so the saints on earth in chapters 6-19 are the church in every generation.

texts.title: The gathering, the apostasy and the restrainer
texts.question: Must the apostasy and the man of lawlessness come before "our gathering together to him", and who is the restrainer?

readings.reading: Paul calms readers who feared they were already in the day of the Lord. Pretribulationists say the restrainer is the Holy Spirit acting through the church, so the church is removed before the lawless one is revealed. Some also read "the falling away" (apostasia) as "the departure", meaning the rapture itself.
Midtribulationists place the revealing of the man of lawlessness in the first half of the week, before the church is gathered at the middle.

Prewrath writers say Paul plainly puts the apostasy and the revealing of the man of lawlessness before the day of the Lord and the gathering. Kurschner argues that believers will see the Antichrist's rise before they are gathered.

Posttribulationists say the "coming" and "gathering" of verse 1 are the same event as the coming that destroys the lawless one (verse 8). The church will see him first. They take the restrainer to be something else, such as God's ordering of the state or the preaching of the gospel.
Partial-rapture writers allow that some believers are gathered before the lawless one is revealed and others later, according to their readiness.

Amillennial and postmillennial writers read the man of lawlessness either as a figure still to come just before the single return (Riddlebarger), or as a first-century figure linked to AD 70 (Gentry). In both, the gathering is the final return of Christ.

texts.title: After the tribulation of those days
texts.question: Is the gathering of the elect "after the tribulation" the rapture of the church, or a gathering of Israel or of saved people at the end?

readings.reading: Pretribulationists say the Olivet Discourse is addressed to the disciples as representatives of Israel. The "elect" are Jews and tribulation believers gathered for the kingdom (compare Isaiah 27:13). The church's rapture is not in view; it is a mystery Paul revealed later.
Midtribulationists also see this as the return to earth at the end of the week, separate from the earlier rapture at the middle.

Prewrath writers see this as the rapture. "The tribulation" here is the Antichrist's great tribulation (24:21), which is cut short (24:22). The cosmic signs then announce the day of the Lord (Joel 2:31), and the elect are gathered before the wrath falls.

This is the central text for posttribulationists. Jesus says the gathering comes "immediately after the tribulation". It has the same trumpet, clouds and angels as 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17. The elect are all believers, including the church.
Partial-rapture writers see this as the last gathering, which takes up believers who were not ready for the earlier rapture.

Preterist one-coming writers read verses 29-31 as the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, told in the language of Old Testament prophecy, with "angels" as messengers of the gospel gathering the nations. Others in this group read them as the final return at the end of the age.

texts.title: One taken, one left
texts.question: Is the one "taken" raptured to safety, or taken away in judgment?

readings.reading: Many pretribulationists say this describes the return to earth, not the rapture. As in the flood (24:39), the ones taken are removed in judgment, and those left enter the kingdom.
Midtribulationists usually follow the pretribulational reading and apply it to the end of the week.
Prewrath writers read "taken" (paralambano, to take along) as taken to be with Christ, the same verb as in John 14:3. Those taken are rescued at the rapture just before the day of the Lord.

Posttribulationists also read "taken" as the gathering of the saints, at the single coming after the tribulation. They note that the passage follows directly from the gathering of the elect in verse 31.
Partial-rapture writers see here a selective removal of the watchful, followed by a warning to "watch" (24:42). Those left are believers who were not ready.

On this view the text describes the one coming as sudden and dividing. Some take the "taken" as gathered to Christ and others as swept away in judgment; either way it is the final return, not a hidden earlier event.

texts.title: The seventh trumpet
texts.question: Does the seventh trumpet mark the middle of the week, the end of the age, or the start of the final bowls?

readings.reading: Pretribulationists say the seventh trumpet is a judgment trumpet on the world, not a gathering trumpet for the church, so it is not Paul's last trumpet. It looks ahead to the bowls and the end of the week.
Midtribulationists see the seventh trumpet as Paul's last trumpet. They link it with the rise of the two witnesses (11:12) and the middle of the week, before the bowls of wrath in chapter 16.
Prewrath writers place the seventh trumpet late in the week, after the rapture at the sixth seal. It announces the final bowls and the reclaiming of the kingdom.

Posttribulationists say the seventh trumpet announces the end: the kingdom of the world becomes Christ's, and the time comes to judge the dead and reward the saints (11:18). That fits the end of the age and a single coming.
Amillennial writers read Revelation in parallel cycles. Each cycle (seals, trumpets, bowls) ends at the final judgment. The seventh trumpet, like the seventh seal and bowl, shows the end of history.

texts.title: The sixth seal: the great day of their wrath has come
texts.question: Does wrath begin at the sixth seal, or was it present from the first seal?

readings.reading: Pretribulationists say the Lamb opens all the seals, so all are his judgments. The people in 6:17 recognize that the wrath "has come", meaning it was already under way. So the whole week is wrath, and the church must be absent from it all.
Midtribulationists see the early seals as human and satanic evil. They place the start of God's wrath later, at the middle of the week.

This is the key text for prewrath. The sixth seal brings the darkened sun and moon that Joel 2:31 says come before the day of the Lord. Only then does the text say the day of wrath has come. The rapture (the great multitude, 7:9-14) comes between this signal and the trumpets.

Posttribulationists see the sixth seal as the cosmic signs at the very end, matching Matthew 24:29. They read the trumpets and bowls as overlapping with or repeating the seals, so the coming follows soon after.
Amillennial writers see the sixth seal as a picture of the final judgment at the one return. The seals cover the whole age from the cross to the end.

texts.title: The seventieth week
texts.question: Is Daniel's seventieth week still future and seven years long, or was it fulfilled in Christ?

readings.reading: Pretribulationists hold that the seventy weeks concern Daniel's people (9:24). A gap separates week 69 from week 70. The church age fills that gap, and the seventieth week resumes God's dealings with Israel, so the church is taken out first.
Midtribulationists agree the week is future. They stress that it divides at the middle, when the covenant is broken, and place the rapture at that point.
Prewrath writers agree the week is future. The abomination at the middle begins the great tribulation; the rapture comes later, when that persecution is cut short, during the second half.
Most posttribulationists accept a future seventieth week, but say Daniel gives no hint that the church is removed. The saints are present under the little horn (Daniel 7:21-22).
Partial-rapture writers accept the future week and see it as a time when unready believers are tested.

Many one-coming writers say the seventieth week was fulfilled in Christ: he confirmed the covenant and made sacrifice cease by his death (Hebrews 10:12-14), with AD 70 following. Others read the seventy weeks symbolically for the whole age. No gap of two thousand years is needed.

arguments.title: Imminence: the Lord could come at any moment
arguments.argument: The New Testament tells believers to wait and watch for Christ himself, not for the Antichrist or the tribulation (Titus 2:13, James 5:8, 1 Thessalonians 1:10). Pretribulationists argue that if a seven-year tribulation had to come first, believers would look for signs, not for Christ. Only a rapture before the tribulation keeps the coming truly imminent.
arguments.counter: Critics answer that "imminent" in the New Testament means near and certain, not "with no events before it". Jesus foretold events before his return, such as Peter's old age (John 21:18-19) and the gospel to all nations (Matthew 24:14). Paul said the day would not come until the apostasy (2 Thessalonians 2:3).
arguments.answer: Pretribulationists reply that those events were either fulfilled early or did not stop the early church from expecting Christ at any time. 2 Thessalonians 2 speaks of the day of the Lord, not of the rapture. Expecting Christ, not the Antichrist, is the posture the epistles teach.

arguments.title: Israel, the church and the seventieth week
arguments.argument: Daniel's seventy weeks are decreed for "your people and your holy city" (Daniel 9:24). Pretribulationists hold that God has distinct programs for Israel and the church. The church began at Pentecost after week 69, and the seventieth week returns to God's plan for Israel (Jeremiah 30:7, "the time of Jacob's trouble"). So the church is taken before the week begins.
arguments.counter: Covenant and posttribulational writers reply that the New Testament makes Jew and Gentile one body (Ephesians 2:14-16) and calls the church the true circumcision (Philippians 3:3). Nothing in Daniel says the church must be absent. Also, believing Jews in the tribulation would themselves be part of the church.
arguments.answer: Pretribulationists answer that unity in Christ does not erase God's national promises (Romans 11:25-29). The tribulation's focus on the twelve tribes (Revelation 7:4-8), the temple and Jerusalem fits a time when God is again dealing with Israel as a nation.

arguments.title: The restrainer is the Spirit in the church
arguments.argument: In 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7 something (neuter) and someone (masculine) holds back the lawless one until "taken out of the way". Pretribulationists argue that only God can restrain Satan's man, and the Holy Spirit dwells in the church (1 Corinthians 3:16). When the church is removed, the Spirit's restraining work through it ends, and the lawless one appears.
arguments.counter: Critics note that Paul never names the restrainer, and early writers such as Tertullian thought it was the Roman Empire. If the Spirit leaves, how are people saved during the tribulation? Gundry and others say the restrainer could be an angel (compare Daniel 10:13) or God's ordering of government.
arguments.answer: Pretribulationists answer that the Spirit is not removed from the world, only his special restraining ministry through the indwelt church. He still works as he did before Pentecost. The neuter and masculine forms both fit the Spirit, since the Greek word for spirit is neuter.

arguments.title: Mortals are needed to enter the millennium
arguments.argument: Isaiah 65:20 and Revelation 20:7-9 show people in the millennium who still die, sin and can rebel. Pretribulationists argue that if all believers are raptured and glorified at the end, and all unbelievers are judged (Matthew 25:31-46), no one in a mortal body is left to enter the kingdom. A pre-tribulation rapture allows people saved during the tribulation to enter it in mortal bodies.
arguments.counter: Posttribulationists answer that mortal survivors can enter the kingdom without a gap: for example, Jews who believe as they see Christ (Zechariah 12:10, Romans 11:26) are converted at his coming and are not raptured. Amillennial writers say the problem only arises for those who expect a future earthly millennium.
arguments.answer: Pretribulationists reply that anyone converted at the coming is a believer and should be raptured with the church under the posttrib model. A gap of time between the rapture and the return is the simplest way to explain who enters the kingdom alive.

arguments.title: The last trumpet is the seventh trumpet
arguments.argument: Paul says the rapture happens at "the last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:52). Revelation numbers its trumpets, and the seventh is the last. Midtribulationists, such as Gleason Archer and Norman Harrison, note that at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God is finished (Revelation 10:7) and the saints are rewarded (11:18). They place it at the middle of the week.
arguments.counter: Critics from both sides say Paul's readers could not have known Revelation's trumpets, so he cannot mean the seventh one. Others note that Revelation 11:15-18 points to the end of the age, not its middle, since it speaks of judging the dead.
arguments.answer: Midtribulationists answer that the Spirit who inspired both books could join them. The seventh trumpet looks ahead to the end, but its sounding is placed before the bowls, which still lie ahead in chapters 15-16.

arguments.title: The two witnesses rise in the middle of the week
arguments.argument: The two witnesses preach 1,260 days, are killed, and then hear "Come up here" and rise in a cloud (Revelation 11:3, 11:12). Midtribulationists see this as a picture of the church's rapture at the middle of the week, just before the seventh trumpet.
arguments.counter: Critics say the witnesses are two individuals (or Israel's witness), not the whole church. Their rising after three and a half days need not fall at the middle of the week. Posttribulationists place their ministry in the second half.
arguments.answer: Midtribulationists answer that the witnesses at least show a pattern: God's people bear witness, then are caught up in a cloud at a trumpet. The timing of 1,260 days fits half the week, and the trumpet follows at once.

arguments.title: Wrath belongs to the second half
arguments.argument: Daniel 9:27, 7:25 and 12:7 divide the week at the middle. Jesus says great tribulation begins with the abomination (Matthew 24:15-21). Midtribulationists argue that the first half is a time of false peace and human evil, while the second half is God's wrath. The church, promised rescue from wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9), is removed at the midpoint.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists say the seals in the first half are already the Lamb's judgments. Prewrath and posttrib writers say the great tribulation in the second half is persecution by the Antichrist, not God's wrath, so the midpoint is not the start of wrath.
arguments.answer: Midtribulationists answer that the seals are general troubles like those Jesus called "the beginning of birth pains" (Matthew 24:8). The midpoint is the most clearly marked break in Daniel and Revelation, so it is the natural place for the church to leave.

arguments.title: Signs before, imminence after
arguments.argument: Midtribulationists argue their view keeps both the New Testament signs and the hope. Believers will see the Antichrist's covenant and rise (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4), which explains why Paul and Jesus give signs to the church. Yet the rapture still comes before God's wrath, so the blessed hope (Titus 2:13) is rescue, not endurance of wrath.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists say any signs before the rapture destroy imminence. Posttribulationists say once the church is told to expect the Antichrist, there is no reason to stop at the middle; the signs Jesus gives (Matthew 24:29-30) come at the very end.
arguments.answer: Midtribulationists answer that imminence means watching expectantly, not that nothing can come first. The middle of the week is the point where Scripture itself marks the turn from man's wrath to God's.

arguments.title: Tribulation is not wrath
arguments.argument: Prewrath writers argue that the New Testament uses "tribulation" (thlipsis) for the suffering believers face from the world (John 16:33, Acts 14:22, Revelation 1:9), and "wrath" (orge) for God's judgment on the wicked. The great tribulation is the Antichrist's war on the saints (Revelation 13:7). The church is promised escape from wrath, not from tribulation.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists answer that the seals are opened by the Lamb and that the whole seventieth week is a single unit of God's judgment (Revelation 6:1). They argue that Jesus' "great tribulation" includes divine judgments, not only persecution.
arguments.answer: Prewrath writers reply that the Lamb opening the seals does not mean every event in them is God's wrath; the fifth seal is the martyrs' cry for vengeance that has not yet come (Revelation 6:10). The text first says wrath "has come" only at the sixth seal (6:17).

arguments.title: Cosmic signs, then the day of the Lord
arguments.argument: Joel 2:31 says the sun will be darkened and the moon turned to blood before the great day of the Lord. Matthew 24:29-31 puts the same signs after the great tribulation and before the gathering of the elect. Revelation 6:12-17 puts them at the sixth seal, just before wrath "has come". Prewrath writers argue that this sequence fixes the rapture after the tribulation is cut short but before the day of the Lord.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists say there may be more than one set of cosmic signs, and that the day of the Lord in Scripture can include the whole period. Posttribulationists say Matthew 24:29 puts the signs after the tribulation, not inside it, so the gathering is at the very end.
arguments.answer: Prewrath writers answer that Jesus said the days would be "cut short" for the elect (Matthew 24:22). So the gathering ends the persecution early, before the end of the week. The order "signs, then wrath" is repeated in three separate texts.

arguments.title: The great multitude arrives in heaven
arguments.argument: Revelation 7:9-14 shows a vast multitude from every nation standing before the throne, who "come out of the great tribulation". It appears after the sixth seal and before the seventh seal opens the trumpets. Prewrath writers see this as the raptured church, arriving suddenly between the signal of wrath and its outpouring.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists say the multitude are those saved and martyred during the tribulation, not the church. Posttribulationists say the scene is a vision of the end that need not fit a timeline. Amillennial writers read it as the whole redeemed people seen at the last day.
arguments.answer: Prewrath writers answer that the group is too large and too sudden to be only martyrs. It appears at the exact place where the sequence of Matthew 24 puts the gathering of the elect.

arguments.title: Believers will see the Antichrist first
arguments.argument: Paul tells believers that the day of the Lord and "our gathering to him" will not come until the apostasy and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:1-4). Jesus warns his followers to flee when they see the abomination (Matthew 24:15-16). Kurschner argues that these warnings are only useful if the church is present to see them.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists answer that 2 Thessalonians 2 concerns the day of the Lord, not the rapture, and that Matthew 24 addresses Jewish believers in Judea. They note that Paul comforts the church rather than preparing it to face the Antichrist.
arguments.answer: Prewrath writers reply that Paul links "the coming" and "our gathering" in one phrase (2:1) and then gives events that come before it. Jesus' warnings are given to the same disciples who received the Great Commission, the founders of the church.

arguments.title: "Immediately after the tribulation"
arguments.argument: Jesus places his coming and the gathering of the elect "immediately after the tribulation of those days" (Matthew 24:29-31). Posttribulationists argue that this is the plainest timing statement in Scripture. The same features appear in 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17: descent, trumpet, clouds and gathering. Ladd and Gundry see no reason to split them.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists say Matthew 24 is about Israel and the elect are tribulation saints. Prewrath writers agree it is the rapture but say "those days" are cut short, so it falls before the end of the week.
arguments.answer: Posttribulationists reply that the disciples who heard the discourse became the church, and the parallels with Paul are too close to be two events. Cutting the days short means God limits the tribulation, not that a gap opens before the end.

arguments.title: Apantesis: meeting to escort the king
arguments.argument: Paul uses apantesis for meeting the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Peterson and others argue it was a term for a city's delegation going out to greet a visiting dignitary and then escorting him back. Luke uses it this way when believers come out to meet Paul and walk with him to Rome (Acts 28:15). So the church rises to meet Christ and returns with him to earth.
arguments.counter: Cosby argues the word was not a fixed technical term. Pretribulationists add that in Matthew 25:6 the virgins meet the bridegroom and go in with him to the feast, not back out. The direction after the meeting must come from context.
arguments.answer: Posttribulationists agree it is not strictly technical, but say the usual pattern is escort, and both Acts 28:15 and Matthew 25:6 show the welcoming party joining the arriving figure at his destination. Christ's destination in 1 Thessalonians 4 is earth.

arguments.title: The New Testament knows one second coming
arguments.argument: The New Testament uses the same words (parousia, apokalypsis, epiphaneia) for the coming that believers hope for and the coming that destroys the lawless one (1 Thessalonians 4:15, 2 Thessalonians 2:8). Hebrews 9:28 speaks of Christ appearing "a second time". Posttribulationists argue that no text clearly describes a coming in two stages seven years apart.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists answer that the same words also describe the first coming, so shared words do not prove a single event. They point to contrasts: a coming for the saints in the air versus with the saints to earth (Zechariah 14:5, Jude 14), a coming with no signs versus one after signs.
arguments.answer: Posttribulationists reply that the "contrasts" are different aspects of one event, as the meeting in the air leads into the return. The burden is on those who see two comings to show a text that teaches it, not one that permits it.

arguments.title: Saints are present in the tribulation
arguments.argument: Revelation repeatedly shows "saints" on earth during the tribulation: the beast makes war on them (13:7), they need endurance (14:12), and they keep the testimony of Jesus (12:17). Daniel 7:21-22 also shows the saints under the little horn until the Ancient of Days comes. Posttribulationists argue that these are the church, which has always grown under persecution.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists say these saints are people converted after the rapture, perhaps through the 144,000 or the two witnesses. The fact that the word "church" does not appear in chapters 4-19 is significant, they argue.
arguments.answer: Posttribulationists answer that "saints" is Paul's normal word for the church (for example 1 Corinthians 1:2). A large new body of believers, saved after the church and the Spirit's restraining work are gone, is harder to explain than the church's presence.

arguments.title: A reward for the watchful
arguments.argument: Jesus tells his disciples to watch and pray "that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things" (Luke 21:36). Hebrews 9:28 says he will appear to those who eagerly wait for him. Partial-rapture writers such as Robert Govett and G. H. Lang argue that the first rapture is a reward for faithful, watchful believers, while others remain to be purified in the tribulation.
arguments.counter: Critics in every camp answer that this makes rapture depend on works. It divides the body of Christ, which Paul says will be changed "all" together (1 Corinthians 15:51). In 1 Thessalonians 5:10 Paul says believers will live with Christ "whether we wake or sleep".
arguments.answer: Partial-rapture writers reply that salvation is by grace, but rewards and the timing of entry into the kingdom depend on faithfulness, as in the parable of the virgins (Matthew 25:1-13). The "all" of 1 Corinthians 15:51 refers to all who are raptured at that time.

arguments.title: Answering the charge of salvation by works
arguments.argument: Critics say partial rapture teaches salvation by works. Partial-rapture writers answer that it does not touch salvation. All believers are saved and will share in the final resurrection. The question is reward: Paul himself strove to "attain" a special resurrection (Philippians 3:11-14), and believers can suffer loss while still being saved (1 Corinthians 3:15).
arguments.counter: Other views reply that Philippians 3:11 speaks of the resurrection all believers share, and 1 Corinthians 3:15 speaks of judging works, not of being left behind. The rapture is part of salvation itself, given to those "in Christ" (1 Thessalonians 4:16), not to the most faithful.
arguments.answer: Partial-rapture writers answer that "in Christ" names the whole group raised at some point, but Scripture also speaks of firstfruits (Revelation 14:4) and of being "counted worthy" (Luke 21:36). God can distinguish timing without distinguishing salvation.

arguments.title: One visible return ends the age
arguments.argument: Amillennial and postmillennial writers note that the New Testament links Christ's one return with the resurrection of all the dead (John 5:28-29), the judgment of all nations (Matthew 25:31-32), and the renewal of creation (2 Peter 3:10-13). They argue there is no room for a secret rapture, a seven-year gap, or a later return. The church is gathered when every eye sees him (Revelation 1:7).
arguments.counter: Premillennialists answer that Revelation 20 places a thousand years between two resurrections. Pretribulationists add that texts which compress events, like Old Testament prophecy, can still describe events separated by time.
arguments.answer: One-coming writers reply that Revelation 20 is a symbolic vision best read through the clearer teaching passages. Jesus says the resurrection of the just and the unjust happens in "an hour" (John 5:28-29), and believers are raised on "the last day" (John 6:40).

arguments.title: The great tribulation was AD 70
arguments.argument: Preterist one-coming writers such as Gentry and Mathison note that Jesus told those in Judea to flee (Matthew 24:16) and said "this generation" would not pass away until these things happened (24:34). Luke says Jerusalem would be surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20). They read the great tribulation as the Roman war and the fall of the temple in AD 70, already past.
arguments.counter: Futurists answer that Jesus calls it the worst tribulation ever, never to be equalled (Matthew 24:21), and connects it directly to his visible return (24:29-30), which has not happened. They take "this generation" to mean the generation that sees these signs.
arguments.answer: Preterists reply that "never to be equalled" is a common prophetic formula (compare Ezekiel 5:9 on the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC). The "coming on the clouds" uses Old Testament judgment language (Isaiah 19:1). The final, bodily return is taught in other passages (Acts 1:11) and is still future.

arguments.title: Tribulation marks the whole age
arguments.argument: Many amillennialists read "tribulation" as the normal experience of the church between Christ's comings (John 16:33, Acts 14:22). John calls himself a partner "in the tribulation" (Revelation 1:9). Hendriksen and Riddlebarger argue that the troubles of Revelation repeat across the whole age, with a short, intense time of evil just before the end, followed by the one return.
arguments.counter: Futurists say this reading flattens specific details, like 1,260 days and 42 months, which point to a defined period. Dispensationalists add that Daniel's seventieth week must be seven literal years if the first sixty-nine weeks were literal.
arguments.answer: Amillennialists answer that Revelation is full of symbolic numbers and that the 1,260 days in Revelation 12 cover the time from Christ's ascension (12:5-6). The seventy weeks are a symbolic period that reach their goal in Christ (Daniel 9:24-27).

arguments.title: The witness of the historic church
arguments.argument: One-coming writers note that the early fathers expected the church to face the Antichrist (Didache 16, Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.25-30). The creeds confess one return of Christ to judge the living and the dead. They argue that a pretribulation rapture as a system emerged only in the 1830s, with John Nelson Darby.
arguments.counter: Pretribulationists answer that truth is settled by Scripture, not by dates. They also point to possible earlier hints, such as Pseudo-Ephraem (possibly 4th-7th century) and Morgan Edwards (1788), though the meaning of these texts is disputed.
arguments.answer: One-coming writers reply that Pseudo-Ephraem most likely speaks of believers being gathered to the Lord in a spiritual sense, not removed before a tribulation; this too is disputed. Even if hints exist, the historic church did not teach two comings.

history.label: Irenaeus and Hippolytus
history.text: Irenaeus of Lyons (about 180) and Hippolytus of Rome (about 204) expected the church to suffer under the Antichrist before Christ returns and raises the righteous. Posttribulationists cite them as the early pattern. Pretribulationists answer that the fathers did not address the question in modern terms.

history.label: Pseudo-Ephraem sermon (disputed)
history.text: A Latin sermon falsely attributed to Ephraem the Syrian, dated between about 373 and 627, says the saints are 'taken to the Lord' before the coming trouble. Some read this as an early pre-tribulation rapture. Others argue it means death or protection and that the text expects believers to face the Antichrist. Its meaning is disputed.

history.label: Morgan Edwards
history.text: Baptist pastor Morgan Edwards, in an essay written as a student in 1742-44 and published in 1788, placed the rapture of the saints about three and a half years before the end. Pretribulationists cite him as a forerunner. Others note his gap is shorter than seven years and could be called mid-tribulational.

history.label: Manuel Lacunza
history.text: The Chilean Jesuit Manuel Lacunza wrote in the 1790s, under the name Juan Josafat Ben-Ezra, and his book was printed in 1812. He taught a future return and placed a short interval between Christ's coming in the air and his arrival on earth. Its link to the later pre-tribulation view is debated.

history.label: Edward Irving and the Albury conferences
history.text: From 1826 to 1830 Henry Drummond hosted prophecy conferences at Albury Park in England. Edward Irving translated Lacunza into English in 1827. These meetings revived premillennial hope in Britain and helped shape the setting in which later rapture teaching grew.

history.label: Margaret MacDonald (disputed influence)
history.text: In 1830 Margaret MacDonald of Port Glasgow, Scotland, described a vision of Christ's coming. Dave MacPherson and others argue it was the source of Darby's pre-tribulation view. Pretribulationists and many historians answer that her vision expects believers to be tested by the Antichrist and that Darby reached his view by his own Bible study. The link is disputed.

history.label: John Nelson Darby
history.text: John Nelson Darby, an Anglican clergyman who joined the Brethren, taught a secret, any-moment rapture distinct from Christ's visible return. He developed the view between about 1827 and 1833, and presented it at the Powerscourt conferences in Ireland (1831-33). It rested on a sharp distinction between Israel and the church.

history.label: Plymouth Brethren divide
history.text: The Brethren spread Darby's teaching through Britain and abroad. Benjamin Wills Newton, a Brethren leader at Plymouth, rejected the secret rapture and held that the church would pass through the tribulation. The 1845-48 dispute between Newton and Darby helped split the movement.

history.label: Robert Govett and the partial rapture
history.text: Robert Govett, an English preacher at Norwich, taught from the 1850s that only watchful believers would be raptured before the tribulation. G. H. Pember, D. M. Panton and later Watchman Nee carried this partial-rapture view forward.

history.label: Niagara Bible Conference divides
history.text: The Niagara Bible Conference (1878-1897) spread premillennial teaching in North America. In the 1890s its leaders split over the rapture. Robert Cameron, Nathaniel West and W. J. Erdman became posttribulational, while James Brookes, A. C. Gaebelein and C. I. Scofield stayed pretribulational. The conference ended in 1897, and a successor gathering in 1901 also failed to unite them.

history.label: The Scofield Reference Bible
history.text: C. I. Scofield's study Bible (1909, revised 1917) placed pre-tribulational and dispensational notes beside the biblical text. It became the most influential channel of the view among English-speaking evangelicals for most of the twentieth century.

history.label: Dallas Theological Seminary
history.text: Lewis Sperry Chafer founded the Evangelical Theological College in 1924, renamed Dallas Theological Seminary in 1936. Through Chafer, John Walvoord, J. Dwight Pentecost and Charles Ryrie it became the leading academic centre of pretribulational teaching.

history.label: George Eldon Ladd, The Blessed Hope
history.text: Ladd, of Fuller Theological Seminary, argued that the New Testament knows one coming of Christ after the tribulation. He linked this to a historic premillennialism free of dispensational distinctives. Walvoord replied in The Rapture Question (1957), and the exchange shaped the modern debate.

history.label: J. Oliver Buswell and the mid-tribulation view
history.text: J. Oliver Buswell, former president of Wheaton College, set out a mid-tribulation rapture at the seventh trumpet in his Systematic Theology (1962-63), following Norman Harrison (1941). Harold Ockenga is sometimes linked with this middle ground, though by 1955 he publicly argued that the church would go through the tribulation.

history.label: Robert Gundry, The Church and the Tribulation
history.text: Robert Gundry gave a detailed exegetical defence of posttribulationism, especially on the Greek of 1 Thessalonians 4 and Revelation 3:10. Pretribulationists such as Walvoord and Ryrie wrote critical replies.

history.label: Three Views on the Rapture (first edition)
history.text: Edited by Richard Reiter, this book set out pre-tribulation (Paul Feinberg), mid-tribulation (Gleason Archer) and post-tribulation (Douglas Moo) views, each with responses. It became a standard textbook for the debate.

history.label: Marvin Rosenthal, The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church
history.text: Rosenthal, formerly with a pretribulational mission to the Jewish people, argued that the church is raptured after the cosmic signs and before the day of the Lord's wrath. The book introduced the prewrath view to a wide audience.

history.label: Robert Van Kampen, The Sign
history.text: Businessman and collector Robert Van Kampen, who had shaped Rosenthal's thinking, set out the prewrath system in full, with charts of Daniel's seventieth week. He followed it with The Rapture Question Answered (1997).

history.label: Left Behind
history.text: Tim LaHaye and Jerry B. Jenkins began a novel series about people left on earth after a pre-tribulation rapture. The books sold tens of millions of copies and made the view widely known in popular culture, though many scholars, including some pretribulationists, questioned their use of fiction for doctrine.

history.label: Three Views on the Rapture (second edition)
history.text: Edited by Alan Hultberg, the new edition replaced the mid-tribulation view with prewrath. Craig Blaising argued for pre-tribulation, Hultberg for prewrath and Douglas Moo for post-tribulation. The change reflected the decline of midtribulationism and the rise of prewrath.

millViews.summary: Amillennialists hold that the thousand years of Revelation 20 is the present age between Christ's first and second comings. Christ reigns now from heaven, and departed believers reign with him. The age ends with one visible return of Christ, one general resurrection and judgment, and the new heavens and new earth. Many prefer the name 'realized millennialism', since they do believe in a millennium, one that is happening now.
millViews.rev20: Revelation 20 begins a new vision that goes back to the start of the church age, as chapters 12 and 17 also do. It does not follow chapter 19 in time. The battle of 20:7-10 is the same final battle as 16:14-16 and 19:17-21, seen again from another angle. Both draw on Ezekiel 38-39.
millViews.satanBound: Satan was bound at Christ's first coming, when Jesus 'bound the strong man' (Matthew 12:29) and cast out the ruler of this world (John 12:31). The binding has one stated purpose: he can no longer deceive the nations. He cannot stop the gospel going to all peoples, or gather the world against the church, until he is released at the end.
millViews.firstResurrection: The first resurrection is spiritual, not bodily. Most amillennialists read it as the believer's soul entering Christ's presence at death to reign with him, since John sees 'souls' (Revelation 20:4). Others read it as the new birth (John 5:24-25). The bodily resurrection of all people comes once, at the end.
millViews.thousand: Symbolic. Revelation uses numbers as symbols, and a thousand is ten times ten times ten, a picture of completeness. It stands for the full period God has set between the two comings of Christ, however long that is.

sequence.label: Present age: Christ reigns from heaven and Satan is bound (the millennium now)
The gospel goes to all nations while good and evil grow together
Satan released for a short time; final rebellion against the church
Visible return of Christ
One general resurrection of the just and the unjust
Final judgment
New heavens and new earth

millViews.shapeNote: Amillennialists expect the gospel to spread to every nation through the whole age, and the church to grow. They also expect evil to ripen alongside it, like wheat and weeds growing together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). Many expect a short time of severe persecution at the very end, when Satan is released. So the line is roughly level: real kingdom growth, but no golden age before the return.
millViews.strengths: It fits the New Testament's simple pattern of two ages divided by one return, with one resurrection and one judgment (John 5:28-29; Matthew 25:31-46). It reads Revelation's numbers and images in a consistent symbolic way. It has had wide support in church history since Augustine, including most Reformation confessions.
millViews.weaknesses: Critics say a Satan locked and sealed in a pit fits poorly with a Satan who prowls now (1 Peter 5:8) and blinds unbelievers (2 Corinthians 4:4). They also argue that 'came to life' in Revelation 20:4-5 must mean the same both times, so a spiritual first and bodily second resurrection is inconsistent. Amillennialists reply that the binding is limited to one purpose, and that John deliberately contrasts two kinds of life.

millViews.summary: Postmillennialists hold that Christ returns after the millennium. Through the preaching of the gospel and the work of the Holy Spirit, most of the world's peoples will be converted. Christ's reign from heaven will bring a long age of righteousness and peace on earth. Christ then returns for one general resurrection and judgment.
millViews.rev20: Many postmillennialists, like amillennialists, read Revelation 20 as the present age from Christ's ascension (Warfield, Gentry). Others read it as a later, golden stage of the church age, after the gospel has overcome the beast (many Puritans, Jonathan Edwards). Either way the reign is Christ's heavenly rule, worked out through the church on earth.
millViews.satanBound: Satan was bound by Christ's death, resurrection and ascension (Matthew 12:29; Colossians 2:15). Because he can no longer deceive the nations, the gospel will progressively win them over the course of the age. The strong man is bound, so his house is being plundered, nation by nation.
millViews.firstResurrection: Spiritual. Most postmillennialists read it as regeneration and union with the risen Christ, who has raised believers and seated them with him (Ephesians 2:5-6; John 5:24-25). Warfield read it as the souls of believers reigning with Christ in heaven. The bodily resurrection of all comes at Christ's one return.
millViews.thousand: Usually symbolic: a long and complete period, probably far longer than a thousand literal years. Gentry compares God owning 'the cattle on a thousand hills' (Psalms 50:10), where the number means 'all'. Some older postmillennialists expected a literal thousand years of gospel triumph at the end of the church age.

sequence.label: Christ enthroned at his resurrection and ascension
Gospel age: the Great Commission advances among the nations
Conversion of most nations, including a large turning of the Jewish people; a long era of peace
Brief final rebellion
Visible return of Christ
General resurrection and final judgment
New heavens and new earth

millViews.shapeNote: Postmillennialists expect the gospel to grow like the mustard seed and the leaven until it fills the world (Matthew 13:31-33). The growth is gradual and uneven, with real setbacks along the way. It comes through preaching, prayer and the Spirit, not by force or politics. Most expect a brief rebellion just before the end, so the rise is not perfectly smooth.
millViews.strengths: It takes seriously the many promises that all nations will worship God, and that Christ must reign until every enemy is under his feet. It gives strong motivation for mission and for faithfulness in every area of life. It was widely held among the Puritans and the leaders of the modern missionary movement, as Iain Murray has shown.
millViews.weaknesses: Critics point to texts that seem to expect persecution, apostasy and lawlessness until the end (Matthew 24:12; Luke 18:8; 2 Timothy 3:1-5). The world wars of the twentieth century weakened the view's appeal. Postmillennialists answer that some of these texts concern the first century, others a brief final rebellion, and that the gospel has in fact spread dramatically across the world.

millViews.summary: Historic premillennialists hold that Christ will return before a future thousand-year reign on earth. The church passes through the final tribulation and is gathered at Christ's single visible return. Believers are raised at his coming and reign with him over the nations; the rest of the dead are raised after the thousand years. It is called 'historic' because forms of it were held by Papias, Justin and Irenaeus, and it does not depend on a dispensational distinction between Israel and the church.
millViews.rev20: Revelation 20 follows chapter 19 in time: Christ's return (19:11-21) is followed by the binding of Satan and the reign of the saints. The beast and the false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire in 19:20, and Satan joins them there later (20:10). Ladd argues that the visions read most naturally as one continuous story.
millViews.satanBound: Satan's binding is future. It begins at Christ's return and is far more complete than any present restraint: he is thrown into the abyss, shut in and sealed, so he cannot deceive the nations at all. Historic premillennialists grant that Satan was defeated at the cross, but say Revelation 20 describes a further stage of that defeat.
millViews.firstResurrection: A bodily resurrection of believers at Christ's return (1 Corinthians 15:23; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). The same verb 'came to life' is used for 'the rest of the dead' in 20:5, which nearly all agree is bodily. Henry Alford famously argued that if one is spiritual and the other bodily in the same passage, language loses its meaning.
millViews.thousand: Many historic premillennialists say the number may be a symbol for a long era, while insisting the era itself is real, earthly and future. Others take it literally. What matters to them is that a real kingdom on earth comes between Christ's return and the eternal state.

sequence.label: Church age: the gospel goes to all nations
Great tribulation and the Antichrist; the church suffers but endures
Return of Christ; believers raised and caught up to meet him
Christ and his saints reign over the earth for a thousand years
Satan released; final rebellion crushed
Resurrection of the rest of the dead and final judgment
New heavens and new earth

millViews.shapeNote: Historic premillennialists expect the gospel to bear real fruit in every nation through the age (Matthew 24:14). They do not expect the church to fail. But they read the New Testament as expecting a final time of great tribulation and falling away before the return. The kingdom's full, open triumph comes only when Christ himself returns.
millViews.strengths: It reads Revelation 19-20 in its most natural order and takes 'came to life' the same way both times. It has strong support in the second-century church. It explains texts that link Christ's coming with his visible rule over the nations, without needing a pretribulation rapture or a sharp Israel-church distinction.
millViews.weaknesses: Critics ask why no New Testament text outside Revelation 20 clearly mentions an earthly kingdom between the return and the end, while many link one resurrection and judgment to the return (John 5:28-29; Matthew 25:31-46). They also ask who the mortal nations in the millennium are. Premillennialists answer that later revelation can clarify earlier texts, and that survivors of the nations enter the kingdom.

millViews.summary: Dispensational premillennialists hold that Christ will return before a literal thousand-year kingdom on earth. In it God fulfils his unconditional promises to national Israel: the land, David's throne in Jerusalem, and Israel's blessing among the nations. Most hold that the church is raptured before a seven-year tribulation, Daniel's seventieth week. Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock) say the Davidic kingdom is already inaugurated in Christ, but still expect a future earthly stage.
millViews.rev20: Revelation is read as mainly future from chapter 4 onward, and chapter 20 follows chapter 19 in strict order. The six mentions of 'a thousand years' are taken in their plain sense. The kingdom fulfils the prophets' picture of a renewed earth under Messiah's reign from Jerusalem.
millViews.satanBound: Future and total. After Christ returns, an angel removes Satan from the earth and seals him in the abyss for a thousand years. Dispensationalists argue that the New Testament shows Satan as very active now: he fills hearts (Acts 5:3), works in the disobedient (Ephesians 2:2), and the whole world lies in his power (1 John 5:19).
millViews.firstResurrection: The bodily resurrection of the righteous, which happens in stages: Christ the firstfruits, the church at the rapture, then Old Testament saints and tribulation martyrs at the start of the kingdom (Daniel 12:2; Revelation 20:4). All who share in it are 'blessed and holy'. The unbelieving dead are raised after the thousand years for the final judgment.
millViews.thousand: Literal: one thousand years. The number is given six times in Revelation 20:2-7, and dispensationalists see no signal in the text that it is a figure. A consistent literal, grammatical and historical method of interpretation (Ryrie) leads them to read it as stated.

sequence.label: Church age
Rapture of the church
Seven-year tribulation (Daniel's seventieth week)
Return of Christ in glory
Thousand-year kingdom on earth; Christ reigns from Jerusalem
Final rebellion and the great white throne judgment
New heavens and new earth

millViews.shapeNote: Dispensationalists expect the church age to end in growing apostasy and moral decline (2 Timothy 3:1-5; 2 Thessalonians 2:3). Yet they stress worldwide evangelism and expect many to be saved, even during the tribulation (Revelation 7:9-14). The line shows the world's general direction, not the church's faithfulness or fruit. The kingdom's universal triumph comes when Christ establishes it at his return.
scholars: Craig A. Blaising and Darrell L. Bock (progressive)
millViews.strengths: It offers a consistent literal reading of both the Old Testament promises to Israel and Revelation 20. It explains texts such as Isaiah 65:20 and Zechariah 14:16-19 that show death and disobedience under Messiah's reign. It has fuelled major missionary, Bible-teaching and Bible-college movements.
millViews.weaknesses: Critics say the system as a whole arose only in the 1830s with Darby, and that its sharp Israel-church distinction does not fit texts that make Jew and Gentile one new people (Ephesians 2:14-16). Sacrifices in a millennial temple (Ezekiel 40-48) seem to conflict with Hebrews 10:18. Dispensationalists reply that premillennialism itself is ancient, and that the sacrifices are memorials or for ceremonial cleansing, not atonement.

millDebates.question: Does Revelation 20 follow chapter 19 in time?

readings.reading: No. Chapter 20 starts a new vision that goes back to the start of the age, as chapter 12 does. The battle in 20:8 uses the same words as 16:14 and 19:19 ('gather them to the war') and draws on Ezekiel 38-39, as 19:17-21 does. So it is one final battle seen twice. Also, if 19:18-21 destroys all the nations, none are left for Satan to deceive in 20:3.

Most modern postmillennialists (Gentry) agree that chapter 20 recapitulates and shows the whole church age from heaven's side. Some older postmillennialists read it as a later stage of the church age, after Christ conquers the beast in chapter 19 by the sword of his mouth (19:15), that is, by his word rather than his bodily return.

Yes. The visions run in order. The beast and false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire in 19:20, and Satan is thrown in later 'where the beast and the false prophet are' (20:10). The binding of Satan completes the defeat of the dragon's allies in chapter 19. Ladd sees this as the natural reading.

Yes, in strict order: return, binding of Satan, kingdom, release, final judgment, new creation. On the 'no nations left' objection, dispensationalists note that 19:21 speaks of the armies gathered against Christ, not every living person. Believing survivors of the tribulation enter the kingdom (Matthew 25:31-34).

Yes. Jesus uses the same word, 'bind', for his victory over Satan in Matthew 12:29, and he speaks of Satan cast out (John 12:31) and fallen (Luke 10:18). The binding in Revelation 20:3 is limited to one purpose: Satan can no longer deceive the nations. He still attacks believers, but he cannot stop the gospel reaching all peoples.

Yes, and the binding grounds postmillennial hope. Christ disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Because the strong man is bound, his house is being plundered: nation after nation will be freed from his deception through the preaching of the gospel.

No. Revelation 20 describes removal, not restraint: Satan is thrown into the abyss, shut in and sealed. Yet Peter and Paul describe him now as roaming and blinding minds (1 Peter 5:8; 2 Corinthians 4:4). Ladd grants that Satan was truly defeated at the cross, but sees Revelation 20 as a further, future stage.

No. Satan is 'the god of this age' (2 Corinthians 4:4) and the whole world lies in his power (1 John 5:19). Waymeyer argues that Revelation 20:3 means Satan stops deceiving the nations entirely, which is plainly not true today. Matthew 12:29 concerns Jesus's power over demons in his ministry, not the event of Revelation 20.

A spiritual resurrection. Many amillennialists read it as the believer's soul going to reign with Christ at death, since John sees 'souls' (20:4); Kline argued that it is the natural counterpart to 'the second death'. Others see the new birth. In John 5:25 Jesus speaks of the spiritually dead hearing his voice 'now', before the bodily resurrection of 5:28-29.

Spiritual, with the stress on regeneration and the believer's share in Christ's present reign (Ephesians 2:6). John 5 shows Jesus himself speaking of two resurrections: a spiritual one now and a bodily one at the last hour. Revelation 20 follows the same pattern.

Bodily. The rest of the dead 'came to life' in 20:5 with the same verb, and that is plainly bodily. As Alford argued, a spiritual first and a bodily second in the same passage makes language meaningless. John 5 marks its shift clearly ('now is' versus 'is coming'), while Revelation 20 gives no such signal.

Bodily. The Greek word for resurrection (anastasis) nearly always means bodily resurrection in the New Testament. The first resurrection is a class rather than one moment: all the righteous, raised before the kingdom in stages. The beheaded martyrs 'came to life' in order to reign; souls in heaven are already alive.

millDebates.question: Are there two bodily resurrections a thousand years apart?

readings.reading: No. Daniel 12:2, John 5:28-29 and Acts 24:15 all speak of the righteous and the wicked raised together, in one 'hour'. Jesus says believers are raised 'on the last day' (John 6:40), which leaves no later day for a second resurrection. The clearer texts should govern a highly symbolic vision.

No. Postmillennialists agree with amillennialists: one general resurrection at the return, followed at once by the judgment of all (Matthew 25:31-46). Paul places 'the end' at Christ's coming (1 Corinthians 15:23-24).

Yes. Daniel and Jesus name both groups but do not say they rise at the same moment, just as the prophets merged Christ's two comings into one picture. The 'hour' of John 5:25 already spans the whole church age, so the 'hour' of 5:28 can span a long period too. Revelation 20 supplies the detail of the thousand-year gap.

Yes. Jesus speaks of 'the resurrection of the just' (Luke 14:14), and Paul longs to attain the resurrection 'from among the dead' (Philippians 3:11), suggesting believers rise apart from the rest. Some follow S. P. Tregelles in reading Daniel 12:2 as two groups raised at different times, a reading most Hebrew scholars dispute.

millDebates.question: Isaiah 65:17-25: is there death in the new heavens and new earth?

readings.reading: Isaiah describes the eternal new creation in terms his hearers could grasp. The line about a hundred-year-old dying young is a poetic way to say death has lost its power: no infant deaths, lives beyond counting. The passage is headed 'new heavens and a new earth' (65:17), which Revelation 21 places after the millennium, so it cannot describe an era of mortals before it.

Gentry and other postmillennialists read Isaiah 65 as the new creation already begun in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17) and growing more visible as the gospel prevails. Long life with lingering death fits a world being transformed but not yet perfected: the later golden age before the return.

Death and sinners (65:20) cannot belong to the eternal state, where death is no more (Revelation 21:4). So Isaiah describes a stage before final perfection, the millennium, which brings the new creation's blessings in part. Like other prophets, Isaiah blends near and final stages into one picture.

A key millennial text. Mortals live in Messiah's kingdom with very long lives, building houses and planting vineyards. Death still occurs, so this is neither heaven nor the eternal state. Isaiah 'telescopes' the kingdom and the new creation that follows it, a pattern dispensationalists call prophetic foreshortening.

millDebates.question: 1 Corinthians 15:23-28: is there an interval after 'then comes the end'?

readings.reading: No. 'Then comes the end' follows Christ's coming directly. Death, the last enemy, is destroyed when believers rise at his coming (15:54-55). So no age of ongoing death can come after the return. Christ's reign 'until' all enemies are subdued (15:25) is his present reign from heaven.

No, and this is a central postmillennial text. Christ reigns now 'until' all enemies are under his feet (Psalms 110:1), and only death is left at the last. So his enemies are progressively subdued in history before he returns, and his return defeats the last enemy, death. Gentry argues this leaves no room for a later earthly millennium.

Yes. Paul gives an order: Christ the firstfruits, 'then' those who are Christ's at his coming, 'then' the end. There has already been a gap of two thousand years between the first two stages. The word for 'then' (eita) can mark another interval, so a reign between his coming and the end fits Paul's pattern. Ladd and Blomberg see the millennium hinted at here.

Yes. The three stages allow a gap between Christ's coming and 'the end', when he hands the kingdom to the Father after reigning. His reign 'until' his enemies are subdued is the millennial reign on earth, and death is finally destroyed after it (Revelation 20:14).

millDebates.question: Does 2 Peter 3 leave room for a millennium?

readings.reading: No. Peter ties together the coming of the Lord, the day of judgment for the ungodly, the burning of the present heavens and earth, and the new heavens and earth (3:7, 10-13). They form one event. There is no room for a thousand-year earthly reign between the return and the new creation.

No. Peter's single 'day of the Lord' brings judgment and new creation together. The delay the scoffers mock is God's patience, so that many will repent (3:9). Postmillennialists see this as fitting a long age of gospel advance before the end. (A few preterist writers apply this chapter to AD 70; most postmillennialists, like Gentry, apply it to the final return.)

Yes. Peter's 'day of the Lord' is a period, not a single day; he himself reminds readers that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years (3:8). The day can begin at Christ's coming and end with the burning of the old order after the millennium. Peter is not giving a full timetable.

Yes. In prophecy the day of the Lord is an extended period. It begins with judgment, includes the kingdom, and ends with the dissolving of the heavens and earth (Revelation 20:11; 21:1). Walvoord and Pentecost place 2 Peter 3:10 at the close of that day, after the millennium.

millDebates.question: What did the early church believe about the millennium?

readings.reading: Amillennialists grant that chiliasm, the hope of a future earthly millennium, was common in the second century (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus). But Justin himself admits many true Christians thought otherwise (Dialogue 80). Charles Hill argues that early non-chiliasts held a coherent hope centred on the intermediate state. Augustine, once a chiliast, taught that the millennium is the church age, and this became the dominant view for over a thousand years.

Postmillennialists grant that their view took full shape later, among the Reformers' heirs and the Puritans. They see its roots in Augustine's present-reign reading and in the early church's hope that the nations would turn to Christ. They note that the early creeds confess one return to judge the living and the dead, with no future earthly millennium.

This is a strength of the view. Papias, who is said to have heard John, as well as Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and Lactantius, expected an earthly kingdom after Christ's return. Justin calls it the belief of Christians who are 'right-minded' in all things. Historic premillennialists argue it declined because of Origen's allegorical method and Augustine's influence, not because of better exegesis.

Dispensationalists claim the early chiliasts as forerunners of their premillennialism. They grant that the fathers did not teach a pretribulation rapture or a full Israel-church distinction; whether Pseudo-Ephraem taught a pretribulation rapture is disputed. They see the eclipse of chiliasm after Augustine as a loss of literal interpretation, later recovered in part.

millDebates.question: Will the gospel conquer the world before Christ returns?
